Debbie Wosskow CBE (Multi-Exit Entrepreneur | NED | Co-chair of the UK’s Invest In Women Taskforce - over £635 million raised to support female-powered businesses | The Better Menopause | PHYT | The Wosskow Method | Channel 4 )
Melinda French Gates wrote something last week that deserves more attention.

She describes how, a century ago, women were drugged unconscious to give birth, tied to the bed if they thrashed, and handed a baby they had no memory of delivering. 

We look back at that now and shudder.

Then she asks the question I haven't been able to get out of my head: will our granddaughters shudder the same way at how we treat menopause today?

Let’s look at where we are…

- For every £ the world spends on medical research, just 5p goes to women's health.
- Only 1/4 women in menopause globally get any treatment at all. The rest are sent home to another sleepless night, joints aching, memory slipping, told it's just their age.

I've spent years building in this space, so let me tell you what the data doesn't quite capture.

The gap isn't only in funding or research labs. It's in the ordinary moment when a woman sits across from her doctor, her whole life unravelling, and walks out with nothing.

No diagnosis. No plan. No hand held out.

Melinda is now putting serious money behind changing that. That matters enormously, and we should all be grateful she's using her platform this way.

But money fills the top of the system slowly.

Women in the thick of it need something in their hands now.

That's the graft I care about, so that’s the problem I’m building The Better Menopause to solve.

We’re focused on doing the unglamorous work of building real solutions for real women, treating midlife as the peak it actually is and not a decline to be managed quietly.

A previous generation refused to accept being knocked out for childbirth, and they changed it.

This generation can do the same for menopause.

So here's my ask:

→ Let’s not wait for the system to catch up. Let’s talk about it, fund it, build it, and demand better from the people who treat you.

The revolution Melinda is calling for only happens if enough of us push. Who's in?

P.S. Read her full, hard-hitting article in the comments

Part of me hopes are granddaughters do shudder because that will mean change has happened, we must all keep advocating for ourselves, each other and better for women’s health

Service leadership at its best, thank you for setting a new standard. 👏🏻

Robyn Cohen (Helping women 40+ reinvent without apology | SVP, Universal Media | Founder, AFTR | Personal Brand Strategist | Keynote Speaker | 30 Women to Watch | — Universal Media — Salt Lake City, UT, United States)
I wrote about this too and did a spotlight on Melinda in my newsletter. As a woman who has been going through perimenopause for the past few years, I can tell you, we are no where near being able to truly understand what we need during this period of our lives. Sure, HRT is a step in the right direction, but there is so much more we can learn so we are truly supported and suffering less.

Peony Li (Founder & CEO at Jude | TEDx Speaker | Dragons’ Den | Young Entrepreneur of the Year 2023 | Pioneering clinical research in bladder health — Jude — London, United Kingdom)
I love seeing Melinda French Gates use her platform to amplify this. It has been overlooked for far too long.

The reality is that women are living longer, but not better. We spend 25% more of our lives in poor health compared to men.  

We cannot change health outcomes without changing how we fund them, yet only 4% of healthcare R&D is dedicated to women’s health!

Better outcomes will come from both medical progress and better-designed services. The unglamorous work of turning awareness into practical support is where real change happens.

The question Melinda poses is the one that stays. Will our granddaughters look back at how we treat menopause today the same way we look back at twilight sleep? That kind of historical reframe is uncomfortable in exactly the right way. 

What strikes me reading this is how much of what women experience in midlife at work, the cognitive fog, the exhaustion, the sense of losing themselves, gets attributed to everything except what is actually happening. The women carrying the most in organisations are often in exactly this stage. And nobody is asking what they need. I'm really glad this conversation is getting louder.

There’s still a real gap between awareness at the top and support at the point of care, and that’s where the change needs to happen fastest.

“Will our granddaughters shudder at how we treat menopause today?” That question stopped me. We didn’t accept being knocked out for childbirth. We don’t have to accept this either.

Fiona Gibb (Founder, Gibb Advisory · Independent counsel for senior leaders, before the decision sets — Gibb Advisory — London, United Kingdom)
The gap between what women need and what they're handed in that moment is the same gap that shows up across the board. Consistently underserved, consistently underestimated. What you're building is the kind of response that actually meets the need rather than announcing it will.

Stephanie Holland (Brand-Led GTM Engineer @ mgsh. | Revenue Bottlenecks → Pipeline Systems | Clay Integration & GTM Architecture | Series A - C | Clay Enterprise Cohort Coach | UK & EMEA — mgsh. — London, United Kingdom)
Absolutely. A few more stats to put the imbalance into greater perspective:

— $2bn+/ year is invested in male pattern balding
— $1bn+/ yr in er*ctile dysfunction
— $648m (2022-2023) women’s health overall
— $230m invested in menopause, even though 100% women go through it

I wish her article wasn't behind a paywall so more could access it.

Gifty Enright (Keynote Speaker | Women’s Leadership Coach | Author of Octopus on a Treadmill | TEDx | NED | Mum — BUSINESSSCOPE CONSULTANCY LTD — United Kingdom, United Kingdom)
That question stopped me too. We often assume progress is inevitable, but history suggests it only happens when enough people decide “good enough” isn't good enough anymore. Future generations may well be baffled that millions of women were expected to navigate menopause with little support while carrying careers, families, and entire organisations on their shoulders. The real scandal isn't menopause. It's how normalised the silence around it became.
